extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, engineers, students, and informed public interested in scientific critique and review)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on how to evaluate claimed periodicities in periodogram/harmonic analysis of time series (and more generally how to test relationships between many candidate factors), emphasizing correct significance testing, replication/continuity checks, and correction for analysis artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schuster periodogram significance (basic statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the data are those of an entirely chance distribution, and the squares of the intensities are plotted in a periodogram, then the average value of an ordinate being a, the probability that a particular ordinate will equal or exceed k a is e^{-k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classical Schuster criterion but it applies only to a single ordinate taken without prior selection (i.e., when no searching/selection across many frequencies has occurred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust for multiple comparisons / selection from many intensities
rubrics_metrics.description: When one picks out the largest from a large number of intensities, it is wrong to compare it with the average intensity as if no selection had occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the distribution/probability of the maximum of the set of independent intensities. Example given: for ~51 independent periods between 5 and 40 years, the chance of at least one intensity >3a is 0.926 (not 0.05). Always account for the number of independent periods when assessing significance (i.e., multiplicity correction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of intensity is only one criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual height of the intensity (the 'test of intensity') is only one, and not necessarily the most important, point for consideration when judging a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very large intensity might still be produced by pure chance when many frequencies are examined; conversely, a modest intensity might represent a real weak periodicity if other evidence supports it. Do not base conclusions on intensity height alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of continuity (split-sample replication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indication of the same period in each half of a sequence when analysed separately ('the test of continuity') is an important criterion of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check whether a period appears in subsegments of the data (e.g., first and second halves). Periods that fail the continuity test may be demoted (Beveridge relegated some high intensities to 'possible' when they failed in either half).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of agreement with other records (independent replication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement of the period with independent sequences or other records is often more important than intensity alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek independent corroboration (other datasets, records from other regions/instruments) to strengthen the case for a periodicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a combination of criteria to classify periodicities
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat periodicities as certain/probable/possible based on multiple tests (intensity, continuity, agreement with other records, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beveridge retained only those periods that showed perfect or fair continuity and (in most cases) agreement with other records; the multiplicity of evidential tests should inform classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute realistic thresholds for significance given number of tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Required multiple of the average intensity a to reduce probability of chance depends on number of independent periods; thresholds like '3a' often insufficient once multiplicity considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example numbers: with 51 independent periods, to have chance <1/20 the largest intensity must be ~6.9a (not 3a); for chance 1/100 need ~7.8a. Use these adjustments rather than naive single-ordinate thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct for amplitude attenuation due to detrending/windowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplitudes for short or very long periods can be diminished by the procedures used to remove secular trend or by the analysis method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply corrections for attenuation (Beveridge notes amplitudes for periods <5 years are diminished and those above ~31 years are diminished by the trend-elimination process). He calculates, e.g., intensity at 35 years should be multiplied by (0.87)^{-2} (~1.3) and at 54 by ~3.8. Account for these when interpreting period heights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating all periodic components as equal when synthesising curves
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing synthetic time-series from detected periods, treating all periodicities as of equal importance can give a poorer fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight periodic components according to their intensities (or other appropriate measures) to obtain a better synthetic fit and higher correlation with observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of selection bias when searching many relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining relationships (e.g., correlation of temperature with many candidate rainfall series), the largest correlation among many random tests will be much larger than the average-by-chance value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the largest observed coefficient with the expected maximum under the null when many comparisons are made (e.g., the probable maximum of 100 coefficients is ~4.01 times the probable value of one). Correct inference must account for multiple testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical claims must account for geometry and scale (example: electrode sparking)
rubrics_metrics.description: General statements (e.g., 'small balls with a given separation break down at a smaller potential than large balls') are not universally true; disruptive voltages depend on electrode size relative to gap and other conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support general claims about physical behaviour with appropriate empirical data across scales; consider counterexamples and parameter regimes (the letter cites Russell's measurements showing different behaviour for different radii and gap sizes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify introduction or use of nonstandard units
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to adopt units (e.g., 'Gilbert', 'Oersted', 'abohm', 'abvolt', 'statvolt') should be justified; international acceptability is a relevant criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a persuasive case for new or localized unit names before expecting international adoption; avoid unnecessary proliferation of unit names without clear advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book evaluation: clarity, exposition, and logical derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the book's exposition is clear and logical and whether derivations are appropriate for the intended audience (e.g., deriving electrodynamic equations from relativity is mathematically logical but may be less convincing to average readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the balance between mathematical rigor and pedagogical persuasion; identify whether methods chosen suit readers' backgrounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book evaluation: completeness and inclusion of relevant discoveries/literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that the work acknowledges and discusses major relevant discoveries and literature (omission of significant finds or key references is a shortcoming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: criticism of a book that omitted mention of Piltdown, Boskop, Talgai, Dubois finds shows bibliographic/completeness importance; ensure up-to-date bibliography and engagement with contemporary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book evaluation: suitability for intended audience / pedagogical usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the book meets the needs of its target audience (e.g., class-book for schools, accessible text for students, useful supplemental manual for instructors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider added material like exercises, specimen forms, practical hints, and whether the level of detail and style are appropriate for students or practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book evaluation: quality and accuracy of illustrations and diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations and diagrams should correctly and clearly represent apparatus and concepts; poor illustrations undermine understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out errors or misleading figures (examples: pendulum that would damage mercury cup; inadequate illustration of a granular transmitter). Recommend improved diagrams where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book evaluation: practical applicability and inclusion of worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Include chapters and sections on practical methods, surveying, cost-estimating, specimen record forms, graduated exercises, etc., to aid students and practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical content drawn from authors' professional practice is valuable; prefer books that combine theory with applied examples and useful graphs/figures (e.g., Kutter's formula graph for sewer discharge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental / observational work: thorough methods and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental/observational studies should use careful methods, be mindful of appropriate media/conditions, and situate findings relative to prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Infusoria studies: avoid studying organisms in unnatural media alone; discuss and cite relevant predecessors (criticism where Jennings's latest edition was missing from bibliography). Emphasise independence of mind and methodological care.

rubrics_metrics.name: School instruction criterion: hands-on/outdoor observational learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of school botany gardens and outdoor lessons for observing animal life (nests, tadpoles, insect life-cycles) enhances instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples: observing bird nests, tadpole development, insect life histories during outdoor lessons engages students and provides direct observational learning opportunities.
